To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the spontaneous pulse rate for a given insulator scales with high energy electrons flux, and with area, and with the size and density of imperfections in the insulator, and that the pulse rates for insulators in the CRRES spacecraft are consistent with these scaling laws.
the pulse rate scales with flux, area and type of material.
Pulse rate increases with the area and the type of insulator, and with high energy electron fluence.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the spontaneous discharge rate of insulators in space.
the spontaneous electrostatic discharge (pulsing) of spacecraft insulators by high energy electrons.
the spontaneous pulsing of spacecraft insulators caused by high energy electrons that penetrate thin surface materials and deposit charge inside spacecraft.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the pulse rate for insulating materials inside a spacecraft can be estimated from CRRES data by multiplying the pulse rate measured on the outside of the spacecraft by the ratio of the insulator's area inside the spacecraft to the insulator's surface area on the spacecraft.
the pulse rate is proportional to the high energy electron flux and the area of the insulator, and is inversely proportional to the thickness of the insulator.
the pulse rate is proportional to the high energy electron flux and to the area and type (e.g. epoxy fiberglass) of the insulator.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the pulse rate for insulating materials inside spacecraft is proportional to the high energy electron flux.
the pulse rate is a strong function of the high energy electron flux and the area and type (i.e., imperfections) of the insulator.
the CRRES data suggest that the spontaneous pulsing rate is a function of the high energy electron flux and the type and amount of insulating materials in the spacecraft.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the pulse rate is very low for insulators that are not exposed to high energy electrons.
insulators inside the spacecraft can be expected to pulse at rates that are similar to the rates measured for CRRES insulator samples that were soaked in vacuum for 6 months.
insulator pulsing is a real and serious problem for spacecraft.
